Watch
WATCH
v.
From Old English wæccan, “to be awake, keep vigil,” cognate with wake. Renders the Greek grēgoreō, “to stay awake, be vigilant,” agrupneō, “to be sleepless,” and nēphō, “to be sober”; and the Hebrew shāqad, “to watch with intent,” and shāmar, “to keep, guard.”

📖 Biblical Definition

To watch is the active spiritual vigilance commanded of every Christian during the long night before his Lord’s return—an alert, sober, prayerful, sentinel posture against the encroachments of the world, the flesh, the devil, and the unexpected hour of the Master’s coming. The figure is martial. Christ’s discourse on the Mount of Olives is its great charter: watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come... therefore be ye also ready: for in such an hour as ye think not the Son of man cometh. The same word is on His lips at Gethsemane: watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation; the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak. Peter, having slept on guard that night, writes years later with the lesson burned in: be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour. Paul charges the elders of Ephesus to watch, knowing that grievous wolves will enter the flock; he charges Timothy to watch in all things, endure afflictions, do the work of an evangelist; he charges all believers to watch ye, stand fast in the faith, quit you like men, be strong. The verb gathers up several distinct duties. There is the watch of personal vigilance against besetting sins and devil-set snares; the watch of corporate vigilance by elders over the flock against wolves and over their own teaching; the watch of prayerful sobriety, by which the soul is kept alert and not dulled by the spirit of the age; and the watch of eschatological readiness, by which the church lives as those who expect the Master at any hour. To lose any one of these watches is to be found asleep at the post the Lord set. To keep them is to be the wise virgin with her lamp trimmed, the faithful servant whom his Lord, when He cometh, shall find so doing.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines WATCH as to look with attention; to keep guard; to be vigilant; in scripture, to be in a state of constant attention to duty and to one’s spiritual interests; to keep awake.

expand to see more

WATCH, v.i. — 1. To be awake; to be or continue without sleep. 2. To be attentive; to look with care; to keep guard; to be vigilant. 3. In scripture, to be in a state of constant attention to duty and to one’s spiritual interests; as, watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation (Matt 26:41).

WATCH, v.t. — To guard; to have in keeping; to tend; as, the shepherd watches his flock; the sentinel watches the camp.

📖 Key Scripture

Matthew 24:42 — "Watch therefore: for ye know not what hour your Lord doth come."

Matthew 26:41 — "Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation: the spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak."

1 Peter 5:8 — "Be sober, be vigilant; because your adversary the devil, as a roaring lion, walketh about, seeking whom he may devour."

Mark 13:35-37 — "Watch ye therefore: for ye know not when the master of the house cometh... Lest coming suddenly he find you sleeping. And what I say unto you I say unto all, Watch."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

Watching is corrupted by the screen-consumption culture that has reassigned the very word to passive media consumption—to watch something now means to spectate, not to keep guard—and by the spiritual dulling of the age that has unlearned the sober, alert, sentinel posture the Bible commands.

expand to see more

The very word watch has been reassigned by the screen-consumption culture of the age. To watch now means to spectate—to consume a show, to look at a screen, to be entertained. The active, alert, sentinel sense of the verb has nearly disappeared from common usage, and with it the moral imagination required to hear Christ’s command to watch therefore as anything more than a metaphor. The believer of the present age is more often watching something than watching for something; the long hours of screen-time have trained the soul into a posture of passive consumption that is the opposite of biblical watchfulness; and the spiritual senses meant to be exercised by alert vigilance have been dulled by the constant flow of media designed to numb them.

Recover the doctrine, and recover the sentinel. The Christian is a soldier on watch in the night, with the enemy active and the Master returning at an unknown hour. He is to be sober, not under the influence of the spirit of the age; vigilant, not lulled by routine; prayerful, not relying on his own strength; ready, not surprised when the cry goes up that the Bridegroom comes. The elder watches over the flock, the parent over the household, the believer over his own heart, and the whole church over her Lord’s appointed hour. To keep these watches is the church’s ordinary discipline; to lose them is to be found asleep at the post when the King returns. The most damning verdict in Christ’s eschatological parables is the one He pronounces on the servant whom the Master cometh and finds sleeping. Recover watchfulness, and the church recovers her soldier’s gait.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek grēgoreō (to stay awake, be vigilant), nēphō (to be sober), and agrupneō (to be sleepless); Hebrew shāqad (to watch with intent) and shāmar (to keep, guard)—the sentinel posture of the church in the long night before her Lord’s return.

expand to see more

Greek grēgoreō (G1127) — to stay awake, be vigilant; the verb of Christ’s eschatological commands to watch.

Greek nēphō (G3525) — to be sober, vigilant; paired with watching in 1 Pet 5:8.

Greek agrupneō (G69) — to be sleepless, watchful; used of elders watching for souls (Heb 13:17).

Hebrew shāqad (H8245) — to watch with intent (the almond branch of Jer 1:11-12).

Usage

"Watching is the active sentinel posture of the church in the long night—sober, alert, prayerful, ready for the unknown hour of her Lord’s return."

"Watch and pray, that ye enter not into temptation—the discipline that Peter neglected at Gethsemane and learned to teach as be sober, be vigilant."

"Screen-consumption culture has reassigned the very verb to passive spectating; the recovery of biblical watching is also the recovery of the soldier’s gait."
